t.1.30.1: Let there be friendship between you and me, O god, as you wish, Puraṃdara. But know that my strength is great and truly irresistible.
t.1.30.2: Indeed, O Śatakratu, the good do not commend this, the praising of one's own strength, nor the proclaiming of one's own virtues by oneself.
t.1.30.3: Regarding you as a friend, and being questioned by you in friendship, I shall speak; for words joined with self-praise ought not to be uttered without good reason.
t.1.30.5: Or I could carry all the worlds, heaped together with their unmoving and moving beings, without growing weary. Know this great strength of mine.
t.1.30.4: With a single quill of my wing, O Śakra, I could bear this earth with its mountains and forests, with its oceans and woodlands, and you as well, clinging to it here.
t.1.30.6: To the hero who had spoken these words, O Śaunaka, the diadem-wearer, best of the glorious, the king of the gods, the lord devoted to the welfare of all beings, said:
t.1.30.8: Garuḍa said: This soma is being carried off by me for a certain purpose; I will not allow anyone at all to take the soma.
t.1.30.7: Accept now my friendship, eternal and supreme. You have no need of the soma; let the soma be given to me, for those to whom your honor would give it would surely torment us.
t.1.30.10: I am pleased with these words that you have spoken here, O egg-born one. Whatever boon you desire from me, take it, O best of birds.
t.1.30.9: But wherever I myself set it down, O thousand-eyed one, you should take it up from there and swiftly carry it away, O lord of the thirty gods.
t.1.30.11: Sūta said: Thus addressed, he replied with these words, mindful of the sons of Kadrū and remembering too the deceit practised on account of his mother's enslavement.
t.1.30.12: Though I am lord over all, I will still do what you ask of me; but let the mighty serpents become my food, O Śakra.
t.1.30.13: Saying "So be it," the slayer of the Dānavas then followed him, having told him, "I shall carry off the Soma once it has been set down."
t.1.30.14: Then Suparṇa swiftly came into his mother's presence, and, as one exceedingly delighted, he spoke these words to all the snakes.
t.1.30.15: This amṛta that I have brought I shall set down for you upon the kuśa grass; having bathed and furnished yourselves with auspicious rites, then partake of it, O serpents.
t.1.30.17: Then the serpents, having replied to him, "So be it," went off to bathe; and Śakra, snatching up the amṛta, went back again to the triple heaven.
t.1.30.16: And from this day forth let this mother of mine be free from slavery. Just as it was spoken by you, this command of yours has been fulfilled by me.
t.1.30.18: Then the serpents, desirous of the soma, came to that place, having bathed, having performed their prayers, and having carried out the auspicious rites, filled with joy.
t.1.30.20: Then, by that act, the tongues of the snakes were split in two; and from the touch of the amṛta those darbha grasses thereupon became sacred.
t.1.30.19: Realizing that it had been stolen and that this had been done by a counter-trick, and thinking, “This is where the soma was placed,” the snakes then licked the darbha grass.
t.1.30.21: Then Suparṇa, supremely delighted, having roamed there in the forest together with his mother, the eater of serpents, highly honored by the birds, of undiminished fame, gladdened Vinatā.
t.1.30.22: The man who always listens to this tale, or recites it in an assembly of the foremost of the twice-born, will without doubt go to heaven, a sharer in merit, through the glorification of the great-souled lord of birds.
